_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 2 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 5 Debugging Together. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order: run it first, two bugs, two heads, say it out loud, programmers do it too. The two debugging chapters are the lesson's own first two rounds, block for block - grow/spin/jump against the goal 'grow, then jump twice', and left/right/spin against 'move left twice, then say hello' - with every block label and the dog's end state taken from the kit (ART.block, ART.run), so the film and the lesson cannot disagree about what a block does. A CROSS NEVER LANDS ON A CHILD: every mark in this film sits on a block or on what the program produced.
title: Debugging Together
subtitle: Grade 2 Computing
objectives: Know how to debug programs so that they will run and will produce the desired output.
Identify the benefits of regularly testing programs throughout their development.
Understand the benefits of working with others when debugging programs.

beats.say: Your program runs, and the dog does the wrong thing. That is a bug.
Run it, find it, fix it, and run it again. Ask a friend to look.
The goal is written at the top: grow, then jump twice.
Here is the program. Run it first and watch what the dog does.
The dog grows. Then it spins. Then it jumps once.
That is not the goal. Watching it told us where to look.
The second block spins. We wanted a jump. That block is the bug.
Take the spin block out. Put a jump block in its place.
Now run it again. Grow, jump, jump. That is what we wanted.
Some programs have two bugs. The goal: move left twice, then say hello.

at.goal: move left twice, then say hello

beats.say: Run it. The dog goes left, then right, then it spins.
The second block goes right. We wanted a second move left.
Fix that block. It is better now. But is it right?
Only running it again can tell you. Left, left, and then a spin.
Still not hello. The last block spins: a second bug.
Fix it, run it again, and the dog says hello. Test after every fix.
Sami has read his program ten times. He cannot see the bug.

at.sami: Sami has read his program ten times

beats.say: Amal looks at it once. Fresh eyes see what tired eyes miss.

at.fresh: Fresh eyes see what tired eyes miss

beats.say: One of you can read the blocks. The other watches the dog.
If you are stuck, press Ask. Your partner gives you a hint.
Asking is not failing. Programmers ask each other all day.
Explaining your program out loud is a way of debugging.
Sami reads his blocks, one at a time. Move right. Jump. Spin.
Spin? We wanted jump. He hears the wrong block himself.
Your ears can catch a bug your eyes walked straight past.
Say each block slowly. Does it match the goal?
Real programmers work in pairs and in teams.
Two of them share one screen. One types, and one watches for bugs.
They read each other's programs, to find bugs the writer missed.
In a games team, one person's whole job is to find bugs.

at.job: whole job is to find bugs

beats.say: Debugging together is how big programs get made. So can you.
Run it first, and find the block that is wrong.

at.find: find the block that is wrong

beats.say: A program can have two bugs, so test after every fix.
Ask a partner to look, and explain your blocks out loud.
Two heads find a bug faster than one.
